name: Tax Structuring and Planning
title: Tax Structuring and Planning
answer: Tax structuring and planning covers the choices a business makes about how it holds assets, where it places entities, and when income and deductions are recognised, so that the tax outcome follows the commercial substance of what the business actually does. It spans entity and holding company design, intercompany pricing, treaty positions, financing arrangements, incentives and credits, and the timing of transactions. It is distinct from evasion, because planning works within the law and depends on disclosure, while evasion hides facts from the authority. In this atlas the topic sits inside tax and jurisdictional compliance, alongside the 215 compliance and regulation pages that track filing, reporting and enforcement obligations.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the ledger and the legal entity register before it runs on any specialist tool. Practitioners draw on the general ledger, intercompany agreements, statutory accounts for each entity, transfer pricing files, tax provision and reporting systems, and a calendar of filing and payment deadlines across every jurisdiction in scope. Entity management platforms hold ownership chains and director records, while tax engines and ERP modules calculate and post the entries that the filings depend on. Document review and data classification are increasingly assisted by software, but the underlying records remain the source of truth.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with facts, mapping how goods, services, intellectual property, capital and people move through the group, and who bears risk and makes decisions. From there the practitioner applies domestic law and any applicable treaty, tests the arrangement against substance and business purpose requirements, and models the effective tax rate under each option. Documentation is prepared contemporaneously, because a position that cannot be supported by records is difficult to defend later. Software helps with extraction, classification and scenario modelling, but the judgement about what is defensible stays with qualified tax advisers.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The risks are concrete, including assessments, penalties and interest, transfer pricing adjustments, permanent establishment findings, and disclosure obligations that can turn a filing error into a public matter. Governance therefore rests on approval trails, version control, clear ownership of each position, and records that show who decided what and on what evidence. Professional privilege, confidentiality and local rules on adviser conduct shape what can be shared and with whom. Nothing in this atlas is legal, tax or financial advice, and readers should treat it as a description of practice rather than a recommendation.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more frequent, more granular reporting and toward tax authorities that read data directly rather than waiting for annual returns. E-invoicing mandates, real-time or near-real-time transaction reporting, country-by-country reporting and global minimum tax rules are pushing structuring decisions closer to the transaction and further from the year-end exercise. Authorities are also using analytics and AI-assisted review to select cases, which raises the value of clean data and consistent documentation. The likely result is less room for arrangements that lack substance and more demand for people who can explain a position clearly and quickly.
